# SEO audit checks

<!-- Generated by scripts/gen-checks-doc.ts. Do not edit by hand. -->

The audit runs 38 checks. 36 are scored and 2 are reported without a score.

## How the score works

Each scored check has a weight, and the weights add up to 150. A pass earns the full weight, a warning earns half and a failure earns nothing. Checks that do not apply are left out of the total. The score is the percentage earned.

Some failures cap the whole score, so tidy tags cannot hide a site that crawlers cannot read:

- **search-crawlers-allowed**: capped at 40 when robots.txt blocks search engines from this site.
- **indexable**: capped at 40 when the homepage is marked noindex.
- **content-in-html**: capped at 60 when the homepage has almost no content in its raw HTML, so crawlers that do not run JavaScript see an empty page.

Grades: A is 90 or more, B is 75 or more, C is 60 or more, D is 40 or more, and F is anything lower.

Checks that run on every sampled page fail when the homepage fails or when at least half the pages fail. Otherwise they warn.

## Crawling and indexing

### https

**Site is served over HTTPS** (weight 6)

Why: Google uses HTTPS as a small ranking signal, and browsers warn visitors about plain HTTP pages.

Fix: Serve the site over HTTPS and redirect every http:// URL to its https:// version with a 301.

### redirect-chain

**No long redirect chain** (weight 2)

Why: Each extra redirect slows the first visit and wastes crawl budget.

Fix: Point links and redirects straight at the final URL, so one hop is the most any URL needs.

### host-consolidation

**www and non-www resolve to one host** (weight 3)

Why: If both versions answer, search engines can see two copies of the site and split its signals.

Fix: Pick one host and 301 the other to it, keeping the path.

### robots-file

**robots.txt is healthy** (weight 3)

Why: Google pauses crawling while robots.txt returns a server error. A missing file is allowed, but it is the standard place to point crawlers at your sitemap.

Fix: Serve a plain text /robots.txt with a 200, and include a Sitemap line. If your app returns its HTML page at this path, add a real file or a route for it.

### search-crawlers-allowed

**Search engines may crawl the site** (weight 10)

Why: A robots.txt block stops search engines reading your pages, which keeps them out of normal results.

Fix: Remove the Disallow rule that blocks these crawlers. A common cause is a staging robots.txt that shipped to production.

### sitemap-found

**A sitemap exists** (weight 5)

Why: A sitemap tells crawlers which URLs matter, and new sites with few inbound links benefit most.

Fix: Generate /sitemap.xml with your canonical URLs and add "Sitemap: https://yoursite.com/sitemap.xml" to robots.txt.

### sitemap-valid

**The sitemap is valid and lists pages** (weight 3)

Why: An empty or broken sitemap gives crawlers nothing to work with.

Fix: Return valid sitemap XML with at least one <url><loc> entry per page.

### sitemap-hosts

**Sitemap URLs use the right domain** (weight 4)

Why: Sitemap URLs on another host are ignored or point crawlers at the wrong site. localhost and placeholder domains are a common build mistake.

Fix: Set your production site URL in the sitemap generator and rebuild.

### sitemap-urls-healthy

**Sitemap URLs are live and indexable** (weight 4)

Why: A sitemap should list only canonical pages that return 200. Errors and redirects there make it less trustworthy.

Fix: Remove redirected, broken and noindex URLs from the sitemap, or fix those pages.

### soft-404

**Missing pages return a real 404** (weight 5)

Why: If unknown URLs return 200, search engines can treat them as soft 404s and may index junk URLs. Single-page apps that fall back to index.html often do this.

Fix: Return a 404 status for unknown routes. On a static host, ship a 404.html instead of rewriting every path to index.html.

### page-status

**Checked pages load** (weight 5)

Why: Pages that return errors cannot be indexed, and links to them waste crawl budget.

Fix: Fix the page, or remove links and sitemap entries that point at it.

### indexable

**Pages are not blocked with noindex** (weight 10)

Why: A noindex in the page or the X-Robots-Tag header removes the page from search results.

Fix: Remove noindex from pages that should rank. Check for a staging flag or a CMS "discourage search engines" setting left on.

### canonical-present

**Pages declare one canonical URL** (weight 4)

Why: A canonical tag tells search engines which URL to index when several show the same content.

Fix: Add one <link rel="canonical" href="https://full-url"> per page, pointing at its preferred URL.

### canonical-target

**Canonicals point at the right page** (weight 6)

Why: A canonical pointing somewhere else asks search engines to drop this page. Pointing every page at the homepage is a common template mistake that can remove them all.

Fix: Build each canonical from the current path, not from a fixed site URL.

### internal-links

**The homepage has crawlable links** (weight 5)

Why: Crawlers find pages through <a href> links. Navigation built only with click handlers leaves the rest of the site undiscovered.

Fix: Use real <a href="/path"> links for navigation, and make sure they are in the HTML the server returns.

## Rendering

### content-in-html

**Content is in the HTML, not only in JavaScript** (weight 10)

Why: Google can run JavaScript, but later and less reliably. Many AI crawlers do not run it at all, so a client-rendered page looks empty to them.

Fix: Use server-side rendering or static generation for pages that should rank. For Vite or Create React App sites, prerender these routes or move them to a framework that does.

### viewport

**Pages have a mobile viewport** (weight 3)

Why: Google indexes the mobile version of pages, and without a viewport tag phones show a zoomed-out desktop layout.

Fix: Add <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">.

### lang

**Pages declare a language** (weight 2)

Why: The lang attribute helps screen readers and browsers handle the page correctly.

Fix: Set <html lang="en"> (or your language) in the root layout.

## Titles and metadata

### title-present

**Pages have a title** (weight 8)

Why: The title is often the headline shown in search results, and a strong clue to what the page is about.

Fix: Give every page a unique, descriptive <title>.

### title-not-placeholder

**Titles are not template defaults** (weight 6)

Why: Titles like "Vite + React" or "Create Next App" tell searchers and search engines nothing. They usually mean the starter template was never edited.

Fix: Replace the default with a title that names the page and the site.

### title-length

**Title length is reasonable** (weight 2)

Why: Google has no fixed limit, but long titles get cut off in results, and very short ones say little. 15 to 65 characters is a sensible guide.

Fix: Rewrite the title so the important words come first and it fits in about 60 characters.

### title-unique

**Titles are unique** (weight 4)

Why: When pages share a title, searchers cannot tell them apart. In client-rendered apps it often means every route ships the same HTML.

Fix: Generate the title from each page or route, not from one shared layout value.

### description-present

**Pages have a meta description** (weight 5)

Why: Google often uses it as the search snippet. It does not directly affect ranking, but a good one earns more clicks.

Fix: Add a <meta name="description"> that sums up the page for a searcher.

### description-not-placeholder

**Descriptions are not template defaults** (weight 4)

Why: Text like "Generated by create next app" can appear as your snippet in search results.

Fix: Replace the default with a real description.

### description-length

**Description length is reasonable** (weight 1)

Why: Google shortens long snippets, and very short ones waste the space. 50 to 165 characters is a sensible guide.

Fix: Rewrite it to fit in about 155 characters, with the key point first.

### description-unique

**Descriptions are unique** (weight 2)

Why: One description repeated across pages gives search engines no help and is more likely to be replaced in results.

Fix: Write a description per page, or leave it out on pages where you cannot.

### h1-present

**Pages have a main heading** (weight 4)

Why: A clear heading helps both readers and search engines understand the page. More than one <h1> is fine, so only a missing or empty one is flagged.

Fix: Add an <h1> that states what the page is about, in the HTML the server returns.

### image-alt

**Images have alt text** (weight 3)

Why: Alt text helps screen reader users and helps search engines understand images. An empty alt="" is correct for decorative images, so only a missing attribute is flagged.

Fix: Add alt text that describes each meaningful image, and alt="" to decorative ones.

### image-dimensions

**Images declare their size** (weight 1)

Why: Width and height let the browser reserve space, which reduces layout shift (a Core Web Vital).

Fix: Add width and height attributes, or use your framework's image component.

### favicon

**The site has a favicon** (weight 1)

Why: Google shows favicons next to mobile and desktop results, and without one your result looks unfinished.

Fix: Add a square icon and link it with <link rel="icon">.

### hreflang

**hreflang tags are well formed** (weight 3)

Why: Broken hreflang tags can be ignored or show the wrong language version in search results.

Fix: Use absolute URLs and valid language codes, and include a tag for the page itself.

## Structured data

### jsonld-valid

**JSON-LD is valid** (weight 4)

Why: One syntax error makes search engines ignore the whole block.

Fix: Generate JSON-LD with JSON.stringify rather than by hand, then check it with Google's Rich Results Test.

### jsonld-present

**The homepage has structured data** (weight 3)

Why: Structured data helps search engines understand who you are, and it makes some pages eligible for rich results. It is not required for AI features or for ranking.

Fix: Add Organization and WebSite JSON-LD to the homepage, with facts that match what the page shows.

## Social sharing

### open-graph

**Pages have Open Graph tags** (weight 3)

Why: These tags control the title, text and image shown when a link is shared on social and chat apps.

Fix: Add og:title, og:description and og:image, with an absolute image URL.

### og-image-reachable

**The share image loads** (weight 2)

Why: A broken or relative og:image gives you a blank link preview.

Fix: Use an absolute URL to an image that returns 200 without a login.

## AI search

### ai-search-crawlers

**AI search crawlers may read the site** (weight 4)

Why: OAI-SearchBot, Claude-SearchBot and PerplexityBot feed AI search answers. Blocking them can keep you out of those answers. This only reads robots.txt, so a block at your CDN or firewall will not show here.

Fix: Allow these crawlers in robots.txt, and check your CDN's bot settings. If the block is deliberate, ignore this finding.

### ai-training-crawlers

**AI training crawler policy** (not scored)

Why: GPTBot, ClaudeBot, Google-Extended and CCBot relate to model training. Blocking them is a business choice and does not remove you from AI search answers, so this is reported but not scored.

Fix: No fix needed. Decide your policy and set it in robots.txt.

### llms-txt

**llms.txt** (not scored)

Why: Google says you do not need new AI text files to appear in its AI features, so this is reported but not scored.

Fix: Optional. Do not expect a ranking or citation gain from it.
